title: Trump Weighs Joining Saudi Strikes as World Condemns Houthi Airport Attack
excerpt: Global condemnation of Saturday's Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid airport grew on Sunday, with Trump saying he may join Saudi strikes against the group, the UN chief denouncing the attack, and Gulf states demanding Security Council action.
body:
• Condemnation rolled in on Sunday after Saturday's Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid airport killed 12 and wounded 309 — the deadliest attack on Saudi soil in over a decade.
  • US President Donald Trump said he will speak with Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and is weighing joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis: "We may. We're gonna look at it."
  • The UN chief, the US, Bahrain, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt and the OIC all condemned the strike; Bahrain demanded UN Security Council action and accountability for the Houthis' backers.
  • Aviation fallout: roughly 580 flights were cancelled on Sunday, European regulators widened their Saudi airspace warning, and the US, UK, Spain and Canada advised citizens to avoid the airport.

Condemnation of Saturday's deadly Houthi missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport swept the world on Sunday, as leaders from Washington to the Gulf and the UN denounced the strike on the passenger terminal. It was the third attack on the airport this week and the deadliest strike on the kingdom in more than a decade.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said Sunday that the dead included four Saudi citizens and foreign nationals from Bangladesh, the United States, Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Palestine and Sudan. The 309 injured included people in critical condition, rushed to hospitals by ambulance and helicopter on Saturday.

A widening global rebuke

US President Donald Trump called the attack "terrible" and said he plans to speak with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Asked whether Washington would join Saudi strikes on the Iran-aligned Houthis, he told reporters: "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed a US citizen was among the dead and condemned the attacks as showing "a blatant disregard for innocent civilian life." UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure violate international law and "must cease immediately."

"I am deeply shocked by and strongly condemn Saturday's lethal attack by the Houthis on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, which reportedly killed 12 people and injured hundreds of civilians."

— António Guterres, UN Secretary-General

Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the attacks violated international law, humanitarian law and the UN Charter, citing breaches of the Chicago Convention on Civil Aviation. It called on the Security Council, ICAO and the international community to take firm measures and hold the attackers — and their supporters — accountable. Qatar, Jordan, Egypt, Syria, the Palestinian Authority, Oman, Cyprus, Somalia and Uruguay also expressed solidarity with Riyadh, while the OIC and the Council of Arab Interior Ministers denounced the strikes.

Strikes spreading beyond Riyadh

Hours after the Saturday attack, coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Maliki said a projectile had fallen near King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, raising fears the wider aviation network is being targeted. The Houthis claimed they had "shut down" the Riyadh airport and declared Saudi airspace a zone of military operations.

The two earlier attacks on the Riyadh airport this week killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial plane, according to Reuters. The coalition confirmed the Houthis were behind Saturday's strike on the passenger terminal, which killed passengers and staff alike.

The stakes for aviation

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, warning of the Houthis' ability to strike deeper inside the kingdom and the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified amid missile, drone and interception activity. Flight-tracking data showed at least 291 flights cancelled over 24 hours, rising to roughly 580 on Sunday, according to Flightradar24. The US, UK, Spain and Canada are advising citizens against using the airport, and several airlines have suspended Saudi flights.

Diaspora angle

The fallout reaches India's large expatriate community in Saudi Arabia, which numbers in the millions: New Delhi has asked Indian nationals to stay alert, and Air India and IndiGo have suspended Riyadh flights, disrupting Diwali travel plans for workers and families.

What's next

The open question is whether the United States moves from words to action. Riyadh has spent 11 years trying to contain the Houthis and is now backing another Yemeni-partner campaign — operation "Yemen's Dawn." But with the conflict spilling across the region since the US-Israel war on Iran began in February, a direct American role would mark a major escalation. Watch for Trump's call with the crown prince and any US naval or air movements.
